text:
Preposition
• Definition: A	phrase	is	a	group	of	words	working	together	that	does
not	have	both	a	subject	and	a	verb.	Phrases	usually	act	as	a	single	part
of	speech.
• Prepositions	can	never	be	alone,	so	it	makes	sense	to	learn	about
prepositions	in	their	phrases.	Any	lone	preposition	is	actually	an
adverb.

They can describe the following
• Which one: The man inside the restaurant is waiting for his date.
• What kind: The bag with the Prada logo is fake.
• Where: We are going to school tomorrow.
• When: She went home after work.
• How: She went home in a taxi.

They can describe the following
• Which one: The man inside the restaurant is waiting for his date.
• What kind: The bag with the Prada logo is fake.
• Where: We are going to school tomorrow.
• When: She went home after work.
• How: She went home in a taxi.

How to find the object of a preposition?
• Ask yourself, “What?” after a preposition.
For example:
He went to sleep early.
We see the preposition “to,” so we ask “to what?”
The answer is “to sleep.”

Object of a Preposition
• The object of a preposition is the noun following the preposition that the preposition is related to.
Examples:
I went to a café.
He bought a new phone for his son.
You can meet me at the mall.

Which one: The man inside the restaurant is waiting for his date.
This sentence shows the relationship between “The man,” and “the restaurant.”

This sentence shows the relationship between

We see the preposition “with,” so we ask, “with what?”
The answer is “with the Prada logo.”

Where:
Where: We are going to school
tomorrow.
This sentence shows the relationship
between “going,” and “school.”
We see the preposition “to,” so we ask,
“to what?”
The answer is “to school.”

When:
When: She went home after work.
This sentence shows the relationship between “home,” and “work.”
We see the preposition “after,” so we ask, “after what?”
The answer is “after work.”

How:
How: She went home in a taxi.
This sentence shows the relationship between “home,” and “a taxi.”
We see the preposition “in,” so we ask, “in what?”
The answer is “in a taxi.”

Preposition of Time “In”
• Parts of days (Morning/Afternoon/Evening/)

• Months (August/September/Etc)

• Centuries

Preposition of Time “On”
• Holidays with the word “day” in them.
I am alone on Valentine’s Day.
I can’t wait to open my gifts on Christmas Day.
• Days of the Week (Monday-Sunday)

• Dates

• Holidays without the word “day” in them.

• Time (noon/midnight/6:00/Etc)

The
Preposition
“Of ”
The preposition "of" is a preposition that is used in different ways. Here are
some common uses and examples of how to use the preposition "of":
Possession or Ownership: "Of" is used to indicate possession or ownership.
Example: "The book of John" (John's book).
Origin or Source: "Of" can indicate the origin or source of something.
Example: "A cup of coffee" (coffee as the source of the cup).
Material: "Of" can denote the material something is made of.
Example: "A house of bricks" (a house made of bricks).
Content: "Of" can be used to show the content or components of
something.
Example: "A bag of apples" (a bag containing apples).
Characteristics or Qualities: "Of" can describe the characteristics or
qualities of something.
Example: "A woman of great intelligence" (a woman with great
intelligence).
Partitive: "Of" is used to express a part or portion of something.
Example: "A piece of cake" (a portion or slice of cake).
Time: "Of" can be used to indicate time relationships, especially in formal or
poetic language.
Example: "The dawn of a new era" (the beginning of a new era).
Cause or Reason: "Of" can express the cause or reason for something.
Example: "I'm tired of studying" (tired because of studying).

Idioms (Unit 6)
• An idiom is a phrase when taken as a whole that
has a meaning you wouldn’t be able to deduce
from the meanings of the individual words.
• The phrase “kill two birds with one stone” is
an example of an idiom.
• Can you guess what it means?

It is not literal. It is figurative
Literal: Meaning exactly what it says.
Figurative: Words or phrases that are
meaningful, but don’t actually mean what it says.

Killing two birds with one stone.
Meaning: To achieve two things with a single action.
Example:
Whenever working out at the gym, I listen to English songs. That way I can kill
two birds with one stone by staying fit and improving my English language skills.

More idiom examples
• Under the weather Meaning: Not feeling well
• Break a leg Meaning: To wish someone good luck
• Once in a blue moon Meaning: Rarely
• The ball is in your court Meaning: A decision is up to you
• You can say that again. Meaning: That is true
• Beat around the bush Meaning: To avoid saying something
• Hit the sack Meaning: To go to bed
• Kick the bucket Meaning: To die
• By the skin of your teeth Meaning: Barely made it

Phrasal Verbs
• A combination of a verb with other words such as a noun, preposition, or an
adverb. (The other words are referred to as “particles” or “tied prepositions.”)
• There are two types of phrasal verbs. (Separable and Inseparable)
• Phrasal verbs are very common in the English language.
• Structure of Phrasal Verbs: Verb + Particle(s)
(In Unit 6 of the textbook, pages 54-59 there is a list of common separable & inseparable phrasal verbs)

Here are some examples of idioms:
1. "Break a leg": This idiom is commonly used to wish someone good luck, especially before a performance or an important
event.
2. "Bite the bullet": This means to face a difficult or unpleasant situation with courage and determination, even though it may be
uncomfortable or painful.
3. "Hit the nail on the head": This idiom means to express something accurately or to be exactly right about something.
4. "Piece of cake": This phrase is used to describe a task or activity that is very easy or simple to accomplish.
5. "Cost an arm and a leg": This idiom indicates that something is extremely expensive or costly.
6. "Under the weather": This means to feel unwell or sick.
7. "Spill the beans": This idiom is used when someone reveals or discloses confidential or secret information.
8. "Barking up the wrong tree": This phrase suggests that someone is pursuing the wrong course of action or directing their
efforts towards an incorrect target.
9. "A dime a dozen": This idiom implies that something is common, abundant, or easy to find.
10. "Let the cat out of the bag": This means to accidentally reveal a secret or disclose information that was supposed to be kept
confidential.
